author: Jakson Gudawela
headline: Bechtel brings Jubail and Ras Al-Khair to a conference about new cities
deck: The industrial cities that built Saudi Arabia's export economy are still being extended, and they rarely share a platform with the destination projects.
excerpt: Iain Thomson attends Saudi Mega Projects for Bechtel on Jubail and Ras Al-Khair, bringing the Kingdom's established industrial programme onto a platform dominated by destination developments.
content:
Among the delivery executives at Saudi Mega Projects in Riyadh, Iain Thomson attends for Bechtel on Jubail and Ras Al-Khair — the industrial cities rather than the destination projects, and a programme measurably older than anything else on the agenda.

Jubail has been under continuous development since the 1970s and is among the largest industrial complexes ever built. Ras Al-Khair, newer, was conceived around minerals processing and now anchors the Kingdom's aluminium and phosphate industries alongside a maritime yard. Both are being extended rather than completed, which gives them a different character from a giga-project with a defined end state.

That difference is the reason their presence is useful on this platform. The destination developments are building assets whose revenue depends on visitors, residents or tenants arriving in anticipated numbers. The industrial cities build capacity against contracted offtake and known commodity markets, which is a more conventional investment proposition and a considerably older one. Their delivery record is the longest available evidence of what Saudi Arabia can build and operate at scale.

Ras Al-Khair also sits at the centre of several supply chains this publication has followed. The steel plate mill under construction with Baoshan Iron and Steel addresses the plate gap that shipbuilding, pressure vessel and energy fabrication have depended on imports to fill. Bahri's order of six bulk carriers from IMI is the Kingdom's first merchant shipbuilding contract. Mawani's lease of port land to ZTT for a subsea cable plant places a data infrastructure component into an industrial minerals port.

Those are the localisation stories that have actually delivered, and they share a characteristic this publication has noted before: they cluster around buyers with continuous replacement demand rather than around the giga-projects themselves. A mill or a smelter consuming reagents and wear parts every month supports a supplier in a way that a construction programme's lumpy demand does not.

The industrial cities also carry the infrastructure obligations that the newer developments are only now discovering — power, water, wastewater, port access and industrial estate services maintained across decades, through commodity cycles and turnarounds. MODON's SAR 3bn commitment to Sudair, which this publication has reported, is the current expression of the same programme.

Bechtel's long involvement is itself a data point on the capability transfer question that recurs across this agenda: a management contractor engaged for decades either builds local capability or substitutes for it, and which of those has happened is a fair question to put to a platform discussing delivery.

Speaker names come from the organiser's published agenda.
